chapters.title: Friction
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces friction as the parallel component of the contact force between two surfaces in contact. It covers the resolution of contact forces into normal and frictional components, and applies these concepts to solve problems involving bodies sliding on rough surfaces.
chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:6_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_1:contact_force_decomposition>> When a book slides across a table, the table pushes back — but which direction does that push actually point? Straight up? At an angle? Let's find out. <<TRACE:surface-line>> <<FOCUS:block>> When two surfaces touch, the tiny charged particles on each surface interact through electromagnetic forces. These add up to produce one single contact force — one object pushing on the other. Here is the key idea: that contact force doesn't have to point straight into the surface. It can point at an angle — like this diagonal arrow. <<TRACE:contact-force-vector>> So we split it into two perpendicular components: one pointing straight into the surface — the normal force N — and one pointing along the surface — that's friction f. <<TRACE:normal-force-vector>> <<TRACE:normal-force-vector>> <<PAUSE:short>> Notice that little square — N and f are exactly perpendicular to each other. The contact force IS their vector combination. Friction is simply the part of the contact force that runs parallel to the surface. <<POINT:right-angle-marker>> <<POINT:right-angle-marker>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:block>> Now let's see this in action. A 400-gram block slides on a rough horizontal surface, and the frictional force on it is 3.0 N. The surface is horizontal and g = 10 m/s squared. First: what is the normal force? <<PAUSE:long>> Since the surface is horizontal and the block isn't accelerating vertically, the normal force exactly balances gravity — so N equals mass times g, which gives 4.0 N. <<WRITE_EQUATION:N = Mg = (0.400\,\text{kg})(10\,\text{m/s}^2) = 4.0\,\text{N}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:normal-force-vector>> The block isn't moving up or down, so vertical forces balance. Normal force N equals mass times g — that's 0.400 kg times 10 — giving N = 4.0 N. The angle the contact force makes with the vertical is found from the ratio of friction to normal force — that's tangent of theta equals three over four, giving 37 degrees. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan\theta = \frac{f}{N} = \frac{3.0}{4.0} = \frac{3}{4} \implies \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) = 37°|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> Now for part (a): tan θ equals friction over normal force — that's 3.0 over 4.0 — so θ equals tan-inverse of three-quarters, which is 37 degrees. That's the angle the contact force makes with the vertical. Since normal force and friction are perpendicular to each other, we use Pythagoras to find the magnitude of the total contact force — root of N squared plus f squared — which gives 5.0 N. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F = \sqrt{N^2 + f^2} = \sqrt{(4.0)^2 + (3.0)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = \sqrt{25} = 5.0\,\text{N}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:contact-force-vector>> For part (b): since N and f are perpendicular, we use Pythagoras. F equals root of N squared plus f squared — root of 16 plus 9 — root of 25 — exactly 5.0 N. That's the magnitude of the total contact force. <<PAUSE:short>> Notice what just happened: a 3-4-5 right triangle! The normal force was 4 N, friction was 3 N, and the contact force came out to exactly 5 N. The contact force is always the hypotenuse. <<TRACE:contact-force-vector>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Let's try a real-world version. You're dragging a heavy suitcase across an airport floor. The floor exerts a contact force on the suitcase. If the normal force is 60 N and friction is 45 N, what is the total contact force? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Same idea: F equals root of 60 squared plus 45 squared — that's root of 3600 plus 2025 — root of 5625 — which is 75 N. And the angle? tan θ equals 45 over 60, so θ equals 37 degrees again. The contact force is 75 N, tilted 37 degrees from vertical. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:contact-force-vector>> So here's the takeaway: every time two surfaces touch, there's one contact force — and it always splits into a normal component perpendicular to the surface and friction parallel to it. Pythagoras connects all three. That's the whole picture.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:6_2>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> If both a box and a block on top of it are moving to the right — same direction — why would friction on the block also point to the right? Shouldn't friction always fight motion? This is exactly where most students trip up, and by the end of this lesson, you'll see it clearly. <<PAUSE:long>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Kinetic friction appears whenever two surfaces are already sliding past each other — the word 'kinetic' literally means moving. The crucial rule: kinetic friction on an object acts opposite to that object's velocity relative to the surface pushing back on it, not opposite to its motion as seen from the ground. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:wheeled-box>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_2:box_on_road>> Let's see exactly why with the box-and-block scenario. Here's a wheeled box rolling to the right on a road, and a small block resting on top — but the block is slipping toward the rear end of the box. <<TRACE:wheeled-box>> <<FOCUS:box-velocity-arrow>> As seen from the road, both the box and the block are moving towards right — but the block's speed is smaller than the box's speed. So from the road, everything heads right. <<POINT:box-velocity-arrow>> <<POINT:box-velocity-arrow>> <<FOCUS:relative-velocity-label>> Now ask: what is the velocity of the block as seen from the box? The box is faster, so from the box's point of view, the block is sliding backward — toward the left. That relative velocity of the block with respect to the box is toward the left. <<TRACE:relative-velocity-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:block-friction-arrow>> Kinetic friction opposes that relative velocity — so the friction on the block due to the box is toward the right. And by Newton's third law, the friction on the box due to the block is toward the left. That's why friction can point in the same direction as absolute motion! <<TRACE:block-friction-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:box-object>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_2:heavy_box_pull>> Now let's nail down the magnitude. Here's Example 6.2 from your book: a heavy box of mass 20 kg is pulled along a horizontal surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the surface is μk = 0.25. What is the friction force? <<FOCUS:normal-force-arrow>> First, the vertical direction. There's no vertical acceleration, so the normal force N must balance the weight exactly — meaning N equals Mg, which is 20 × 9.8. <<TRACE:normal-force-arrow>> Kinetic friction equals the coefficient of kinetic friction multiplied by the normal force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f_k = \mu_k N|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:friction-force-arrow>> Now the formula: kinetic friction equals μk times N. Since N equals Mg, we get fk = μk × Mg = 0.25 × 20 × 9.8 = 49 N. This force acts in the direction opposite to the pull. <<TRACE:friction-force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because there is no vertical acceleration, N equals Mg, so we can substitute and multiply the numbers out to get 49 N. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f_k = \mu_k Mg = 0.25 \times 20 \times 9.8 = 49\text{ N}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Quick real-world check: imagine you're sliding a 5 kg carton of groceries across a kitchen floor where μk = 0.4. No vertical acceleration, so N = Mg = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N. The kinetic friction is 0.4 × 49 = 19.6 N — that's the force the floor pushes back on the carton as you slide it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> One more: picture a cricket fielder sliding on the outfield grass to stop a ball. His boot slides forward. The grass applies kinetic friction on the boot — opposite to the boot's velocity relative to the grass, which is backward. So friction points backward, slowing him down. What direction is the friction the boot exerts on the grass? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Forward — opposite to the grass's velocity relative to the boot. The grass, from the boot's view, moves backward, so friction on the grass points forward. Same logic, same rule: always look at the relative velocity between the two surfaces. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So here's the whole picture in one breath: kinetic friction resists relative sliding — its direction is opposite to the relative velocity of one surface against the other, and its size is fk = μk × N, where N equals Mg whenever there is no vertical acceleration. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:6_3>>
<<FOCUS:wardrobe-block>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_3:wardrobe_static>> Here's something strange — you push a giant wardrobe with all your strength, but it doesn't move even a millimetre. You're exerting a real force. So why doesn't Newton's second law send it flying? The wardrobe sits perfectly still. Newton's first law says: if acceleration is zero, the net force must be zero. The workers push it left — so the floor must be pushing back right with exactly the same force. <<TRACE:push-force-arrow>> <<POINT:push-force-arrow>> <<FOCUS:friction-arrow>> That rightward push from the floor is static friction — and here's what makes it remarkable: it adjusted itself to match the workers' push exactly, without anyone telling it to. <<PAUSE:short>> Push gently — friction is small. Push harder — friction grows to match. Static friction is self-adjusting. But it can't keep growing forever. Push beyond a certain limit, and the wardrobe finally slides. <<POINT:push-force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:boy-block>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_3:boy_on_horse>> Now let's meet Arjun — a 30 kg boy riding his horse. The horse suddenly speeds up at 2.0 m/s². Arjun doesn't slide off. What force is actually moving him forward? <<PAUSE:long>> The only horizontal force on Arjun is static friction from the horse's back — there's nothing else pushing him forward. So friction alone must produce his acceleration. <<TRACE:boy-friction-arrow>> <<POINT:boy-friction-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:boy-friction-arrow>> Using Newton's second law: friction equals mass times acceleration — that's 30 kg times 2.0 m/s², giving a static friction force of exactly 60 N. Since friction is the only horizontal force, it must equal mass times acceleration — that's Newton's second law applied straight to Arjun. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f_s = Ma = (30\,\text{kg})(2.0\,\text{m/s}^2) = 60\,\text{N}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now the second part — what if Arjun does slide back? That means the required 60 N was MORE than the maximum static friction the horse could provide. <<POINT:boy-normal-arrow>> <<FOCUS:boy-weight-arrow>> The maximum static friction equals mu-s times the normal force N. Since Arjun's weight is 30 times 10 equals 300 N, and N equals 300 N, maximum static friction is mu-s times 300 N. <<PAUSE:short>> The maximum static friction is mu-s times the normal force. If sliding occurs, that maximum was less than the 60 N required, so mu-s must be less than 0.20. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s Mg < 60\,\text{N} \implies \mu_s < 0.20|id=eq-2|boxed>> For Arjun to slide, that maximum must be less than 60 N — so mu-s times 300 must be less than 60 — which means mu-s is less than 0.20. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Quick real-world check: imagine a 5 kg book resting on a table. You push it with 8 N but it doesn't move. What is the static friction force right now? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Exactly 8 N — friction self-adjusted to match your push. No calculation needed beyond Newton's first law: net force is zero, so friction equals applied force. One more: a 10 kg delivery crate sits in the back of a van. The van brakes sharply, decelerating at 3 m/s². The crate doesn't slide. What's the static friction on the crate, and is that even possible if mu-s is 0.4? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The friction needed is mass times acceleration: 10 times 3 equals 30 N. The maximum available is 0.4 times mg equals 0.4 times 100 equals 40 N. Since 30 N is less than 40 N, yes — static friction is strong enough, and the crate stays put. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:6_4>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's something that might surprise you: it doesn't matter whether two surfaces are touching over a tiny patch or a huge one — the friction force is exactly the same. Bigger contact area, same friction. How is that possible? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_4:friction_laws_diagram>> Let's build up the rules — the Laws of Friction — one by one, starting with the most useful one: what happens when two surfaces are already sliding against each other. <<TRACE:sliding-block>> <<FOCUS:normal-force-arrow>> When surfaces slide, we call it kinetic friction. That friction force depends on two things: how hard the surfaces are pressing together — that's the normal force N — and how grippy those surfaces are, captured by a number called the coefficient of kinetic friction, µk. <<POINT:normal-force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> Multiply how hard the surfaces press together by how grippy they are — that product is the kinetic friction force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f_k = \mu_k N|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:kinetic-friction-arrow>> Multiply those two together and you get the kinetic friction force: fk equals µk times N. Steel on ice gives a tiny µk, rubber on rough concrete gives a large one — the surfaces decide the number, and the number scales with how hard they press. <<PAUSE:short>> Now, which direction does kinetic friction act? It always opposes the motion — if the block slides to the right, friction pulls it back to the left. Friction fights the slide, it never helps it. <<TRACE:kinetic-friction-arrow>> <<POINT:kinetic-friction-arrow>> What if the surfaces are NOT sliding? Then we have static friction, and it's even more flexible — it can be anything from zero up to a maximum of µs times N. It adjusts itself to exactly cancel whatever force is trying to cause slipping. Static friction can be anything up to a ceiling: the coefficient of static friction times the normal force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f_s \leq \mu_s N|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:wide-block>> Now here's the big question I opened with — does a wider block, with more surface touching the floor, experience more friction? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:equal-friction-label>> No — it doesn't. Look: both blocks have the same weight pressing down, so the same normal force N. The formula fk equals µk N doesn't care about area at all. More contact area, but the same N, gives the same friction. The area drops out completely. <<POINT:equal-friction-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> This is why a racing tyre and a thin bicycle tyre — pressed onto the road with the same force — experience the same friction. Counterintuitive, but that's the law. <<POINT:equal-friction-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So let's lock in the four laws: one — sliding surfaces obey fk equals µk N; two — kinetic friction always opposes the velocity; three — non-sliding surfaces obey fs is at most µs N, adjusting to prevent slipping; four — none of this depends on contact area, only on N.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:6_5>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> A steel plate looks perfectly smooth — you can almost see your reflection in it. So why does anything rubbing across it feel any resistance at all? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_5:atomic_surface_diagram>> The answer lives in a world too small to see. Every surface — even the most polished metal — is a mountain range at the atomic scale. Peaks, valleys, craters everywhere. <<TRACE:surface-a-profile>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:surface-b-profile>> Now put two of those surfaces together. They don't actually touch everywhere — only where the tallest peaks of one happen to meet the tallest peaks of the other. <<TRACE:surface-b-profile>> The real area in contact is much, much smaller than the total surface area you can see. <<POINT:total-area-brace>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:contact-points>> At those tiny contact points, the atoms of the two surfaces are squeezed incredibly close together — close enough for molecular forces to kick in. Bonds form. The two surfaces are literally glued together at thousands of invisible spots. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the deep question: when you push one surface sideways, what actually has to happen? <<POINT:molecular-bond-markers>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:molecular-bond-markers>> Every single one of those molecular bonds has to be broken. The material at each contact point gets deformed, then new bonds form at the next set of peaks. Break, deform, re-bond — over and over. That is friction. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And all that breaking and deforming sends tiny vibration waves rippling through both objects. Those vibrations eventually die down — but where does the energy go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It becomes heat. The random motion of particles inside the material speeds up. That's why your hands get warm when you rub them together — friction is literally converting your effort into molecular chaos. <<FOCUS:surface-a-profile>> So remember the two big ideas: one, surfaces that look flat are secretly mountain ranges — contact is only at a few tiny peaks. Two, friction is the work of breaking molecular bonds at those peaks, and that work shows up as heat. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:0_04>>
<<FOCUS:macro-glass-block-top>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:0_04:glass_surfaces_diagram>> Glass feels perfectly smooth — so two glass surfaces rubbing together should slip easily, right? Actually, glass on glass grips harder than most people expect. Here's why. <<FOCUS:macro-glass-block-bottom>> Here are two glass blocks. To your eye — and to your fingertip — they look and feel completely flat. No bumps, no texture, nothing to grab onto. So here's the honest question: if both surfaces look this smooth, why wouldn't they just glide over each other with almost zero friction? <<POINT:macro-glass-block-top>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:zoom-callout>> Because what you see is not what's really there. Let's zoom in on that contact edge. <<TRACE:zoom-callout>> At the microscopic level, the surface of glass is actually covered in tiny ridges, bumps, and valleys — nothing like the flat sheet your eye sees. <<TRACE:micro-bumps-top>> <<PAUSE:short>> And the bottom glass is the same — its own set of jagged micro-peaks, pointing upward. <<TRACE:micro-bumps-bottom>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:interlock-highlight>> When you press them together, those peaks from each surface dig into each other — they interlock. That mechanical gripping is exactly what friction is. <<PAUSE:short>> So glass on glass has a coefficient of friction of 0.04 — which sounds small, but is surprisingly high for something we think of as slippery. <<PAUSE:short>> We give this gripping tendency a number — the coefficient of friction. For glass on glass, that number is 0.04. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mu_{\text{glass-glass}} = 0.04|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> This is the key lesson: friction does not care how smooth something looks. It cares about what is happening at the scale your eye cannot reach. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:0_7>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's a strange question — if ice is already slippery, what happens when you slide ice on ice? Does it get twice as slippery, or does something else entirely explain why ice on ice is one of the lowest-friction combinations we know? <<FOCUS:bottom-ice-surface>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:0_7:ice_on_ice>> Most surfaces, when you press them together and try to slide one across the other, grip because their rough peaks interlock. Ice already has fewer of those jagged peaks than most materials — but the real magic happens at the very boundary between the two icy surfaces. <<FOCUS:top-ice-block>> So here's the honest question worth sitting with: why is ice slippery at all? It's not simply because it's hard and smooth — glass is also hard and smooth, and glass on glass is NOT nearly this slippery. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:water-film-layer>> The answer is that ice is unique — the pressure and slight warmth at the contact point causes the very surface of the ice to melt into a microscopically thin film of liquid water, right at the interface. <<TRACE:water-film-layer>> <<PAUSE:short>> Watch those pressure arrows pushing down — that tiny squeeze between the two ice blocks is enough to nudge the melting point just enough, and liquid water appears exactly where the surfaces meet. <<POINT:pressure-arrows>> <<FOCUS:water-film-layer>> And liquid water between two surfaces? That's a lubricant. The two ice blocks are now, in effect, separated by a film of water — so they're not really rubbing ice on ice at all, they're gliding on water. <<PAUSE:short>> This is why ice on ice gives some of the lowest friction values we observe in everyday materials — not because ice itself is frictionless, but because ice creates its own lubricant the moment you press two pieces together. <<POINT:water-film-layer>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Think about ice skating — the blade presses hard on the ice, that pressure melts a thin layer, and the skater glides on water, not ice. Remove the pressure, the film refreezes in microseconds. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:water-film-layer>> So the crucial idea to carry away: ice's slipperiness is not a property of the solid ice itself — it is a property of the liquid water film that ice produces at its surface under pressure. That film is everything. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:0_10>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's a strange question: what if making a surface MORE pure — cleaner than anything you've ever touched — actually made it HARDER to slide across? Cleaner should mean less friction, right? Well, prepare to have your intuition flipped. <<FOCUS:vacuum-chamber>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:0_10:copper_experiment>> We think of friction as coming from roughness — little bumps catching on each other. But friction has a hidden ingredient: the chemistry of what is actually sitting on the surface. Dust, tiny impurities, and oxidation — the thin chemical film that forms when metal meets air — all play a massive role. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:copper-block-left>> Let's do a thought experiment that physicists have actually carried out. Take two blocks of pure copper — not ordinary copper, but copper cleaned so carefully that every speck of dust and every trace of oxide layer is removed from the surfaces. <<POINT:copper-block-left>> <<FOCUS:vacuum-chamber>> The blocks are also heated to push out any gases dissolved inside the metal. Then both blocks are placed in contact inside an evacuated chamber — a container from which nearly all the air has been pumped out — at a very low pressure. <<TRACE:vacuum-chamber>> <<FOCUS:contact-zone>> Now here's the question — what do you think happens when those two ultra-clean copper surfaces touch each other in that vacuum? Do they slide easily, or something else entirely? <<POINT:contact-zone>> <<PAUSE:long>> The friction coefficient — the number that tells us how hard it is to slide one surface over another — shoots way past one, which is already unusually high for most everyday surfaces. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mu \gg 1|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> They STICK. The blocks fuse together so strongly that a huge force is needed just to slide one over the other. The friction coefficient — the number that tells us how hard sliding is — becomes much larger than one. That's extraordinary; most everyday surfaces have a friction coefficient well below one. <<TRACE:friction-coeff-label-high>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:contact-zone>> Why? Because normally, that thin oxide layer acts like a buffer — a chemical 'padding' between the two metal surfaces. Strip it away, and the copper atoms on each block can get so close they actually bond with each other across the interface. The surfaces almost become one piece of metal. <<TRACE:contact-zone>> <<FOCUS:air-inlet-arrow>> Now watch what happens next. A small amount of air is let into the chamber. <<POINT:air-inlet-arrow>> <<FOCUS:oxide-layer-left>> That oxygen reacts with the copper surfaces almost immediately, forming a fresh, thin oxide layer on each block. And just like that, the friction coefficient drops back to normal values — the same ordinary numbers you'd measure in any everyday experiment. <<TRACE:oxide-layer-left>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:friction-coeff-label-normal>> So the oxide layer — that thing you might think of as 'dirt' on a metal — is actually a natural lubricant keeping surfaces from fusing. Dust, impurities, and oxidation don't just sit there; they fundamentally control the friction coefficient. <<POINT:friction-coeff-label-normal>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's a real-world echo of the same idea. Think about the brake discs on a bicycle or a car. If you leave a steel disc unused for a few days, a thin rust — iron oxide — forms on it. When you first brake, that rough oxide layer actually gives you MORE friction than a perfectly polished disc would in a vacuum. Engineers designing brakes in normal air conditions rely on this surface chemistry — not just the geometry of the disc — to hit their target friction values. <<PAUSE:short>> So the one-line takeaway: friction is not purely about shape and roughness — it is a surface chemistry story. Strip away every impurity in a vacuum and copper seizes up with a friction coefficient way above one. Let chemistry back in, and order is restored. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:0_35>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Why does an egg slide so effortlessly off a non-stick pan, even without any oil — what is that coating actually doing? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:0_35:teflon_friction_comparison>> That coating is Teflon — and it holds a remarkable title: one of the lowest coefficients of friction of any solid material ever discovered. <<TRACE:teflon-surface-profile>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:normal-surface-profile>> Here is a cross-section of a typical solid surface zoomed in to the microscopic scale — look at all those jagged peaks and valleys. When another surface presses down on this, those peaks interlock and resist sliding. <<TRACE:normal-surface-profile>> <<FOCUS:teflon-surface-profile>> Now look at Teflon. At the same microscopic zoom, the surface is almost perfectly flat. There are barely any peaks for another surface to catch on. <<TRACE:teflon-surface-profile>> So here is the real question — if ALL solid surfaces look rough under a microscope, how did chemists manage to make Teflon so uniquely smooth and slippery? <<POINT:teflon-surface-profile>> <<PAUSE:long>> The number that measures how slippery a surface is — the coefficient of friction — is about 0.04 for Teflon, compared to 0.5 or more for most everyday materials. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mu_{\text{Teflon}} \approx 0.04|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:teflon-surface-profile>> The answer is in Teflon's chemistry: its molecules are made of carbon atoms shielded by a tight shell of fluorine atoms. Fluorine grips onto carbon so strongly that it leaves nothing exposed for other molecules to grab — the surface becomes chemically inert and atomically smooth. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mu-label-normal>> A typical material — wood on wood, rubber on tarmac — has a coefficient of friction somewhere between 0.5 and 0.8. Teflon sits at around 0.04. That is more than ten times slipperier. <<POINT:mu-label-normal>> <<FOCUS:sliding-block-normal>> Watch what that means in practice: on the normal surface, the friction arrow on our block is bold and large — a real force fighting the slide. On the Teflon surface, that same arrow almost vanishes. <<TRACE:sliding-block-normal>> <<POINT:sliding-block-normal>> <<FOCUS:mu-label-teflon>> And on the Teflon side — almost nothing. The friction force is there, but barely. That is what μ ≈ 0.04 looks like. <<POINT:mu-label-teflon>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sliding-block-teflon>> So the next time you slide an egg across that pan, you are witnessing atomic-scale engineering: a surface so chemically sealed and smooth that friction has almost nowhere to take hold. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:friction:0_40>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Why does your car need a much longer distance to stop when it's raining — even if you brake just as hard as on a dry day? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:tyre-rubber>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:0_40:tyre_wet_road>> The answer is hidden right at the contact patch — the tiny zone where your tyre actually touches the road. That's exactly what the coefficient of friction tells us. <<POINT:mu-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mu-label>> For rubber tyre on dry concrete, that coefficient is 1.00 — which means the friction force can be as large as the full weight of the car pressing down. Rubber on dry concrete at 1.00 is in a league of its own. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:friction-force-arrow>> This is why tyre engineers obsess over rubber compounds and road surfaces — that coefficient of 1.00 is the reason your car can stop quickly and safely on a dry day.

Is it closer to ice on ice, or rubber on concrete? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:brass-surface>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:1_60:steel_brass_friction>> Let's build the picture. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_6:incline_diagram>> A wooden block sits perfectly still on a tilted board at 17 degrees — then you nudge the angle to 18 degrees and it suddenly slides away. Why does that one tiny degree make all the difference? The answer lets you measure friction with nothing but a ruler and a protractor. <<TRACE:incline-surface>> <<FOCUS:block-on-incline>> Here is the block on the slope. Gravity pulls it straight down with force mg. That force splits into two parts: one pushing the block into the slope — that's mg cosθ, creating the normal force — and one trying to drag it down the slope, which is mg sinθ. <<TRACE:block-on-incline>> <<TRACE:block-on-incline>> <<FOCUS:friction-vector>> Friction fights back up the slope. As long as the block is still, friction equals mg sinθ exactly. The moment friction hits its maximum — µs times N — the block is on the verge of slipping. <<POINT:friction-vector>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle-label>> At that magic threshold angle, µs × mg cosθ = mg sinθ. The mg cancels, and you're left with µs = sinθ / cosθ — which is simply the tangent of θ. The coefficient of static friction IS the tangent of the slipping angle. <<PAUSE:short>> At the slipping angle, friction exactly balances the slope-component of gravity — divide them and the mg cancels, leaving just the tangent of the angle. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mu_s = \tan\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:incline-surface>> Now for the classic experiment — Example 6.4. A wooden block starts slipping when the plank reaches 18 degrees. Once it's moving, the block slides at uniform speed when the angle is reduced to 15 degrees. What are the two friction coefficients? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The coefficient of static friction equals tangent of 18 degrees — that's the slipping angle. The coefficient of kinetic friction equals tangent of 15 degrees — the constant-speed angle. Two angles, two numbers, no extra equipment needed. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:block-on-incline>> Now a question: if µs equals 0.3, what is the maximum angle θ before the block slips? And if the incline is only at θ divided by 2, what friction force acts on the block? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:parallel-component>> For part (a): at the maximum angle, limiting equilibrium means f equals µs N. Perpendicular to slope: N equals mg cosθ. Parallel to slope: f equals mg sinθ. So µs times mg cosθ equals mg sinθ, giving tanθ equals 0.3, so θ equals inverse tangent of 0.3. <<POINT:parallel-component>> <<POINT:parallel-component>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:friction-vector>> For part (b): at angle θ divided by 2, the block is still stationary — so friction is not at its limit. Static friction just equals the gravitational pull down the slope: f equals mg times sine of θ divided by 2. No coefficient needed here — just equilibrium. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Next, a 4 kg block on a rough table. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied but the block does not move. What friction force does the table exert, and what can we say about µs? With g equals 10 metres per second squared, the weight is 40 N. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Since the block is at rest, horizontal balance gives friction force equals 20 N, and vertical balance gives normal force equals 40 N. Because static friction hasn't reached its limit yet, µs is greater than or equal to f divided by N, so µs is greater than or equal to 0.5. <<FOCUS:table-block>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:6_6:pulley_table_diagram>> Now the pulley-and-table apparatus. A 2 kg block sits on a table — µs equals 0.2. A hanging mass m is connected by a string over a frictionless pulley. What is the maximum m before everything slides? <<TRACE:table-block>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:tension-arrow>> The hanging mass gives tension T equals mg. On the table block: normal force N equals 20 N. Maximum friction equals µs times N equals 0.2 times 20 equals 4 N. So T must not exceed 4 N, meaning mg must be at most 4 N, giving maximum m equals 0.4 kg. <<POINT:tension-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:friction-arrow>> Notice what just happened: the hanging weight W2 is exactly equal to the friction force on the table block W1. In the horizontal-table lab method, µs equals W2 divided by W1 — the hanger weight divided by the block weight. That's the whole experiment. <<PAUSE:short>> In the pulley apparatus, the hanging weight equals the friction force and the block weight equals the normal force — so the ratio is directly the friction coefficient. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mu_s = \frac{W_2}{W_1}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Now two stacked blocks: mass m on top of mass M on a smooth table. What maximum force F can push both blocks together without the upper block sliding? The only horizontal force on m is friction from M. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Both blocks share the same acceleration a. For m: friction f equals m times a, and at the limit f equals µ times mg, so maximum a equals µg. For the whole system: F equals the total mass times a, giving maximum F equals µg times the quantity M plus m. <<FOCUS:parallel-component>> A block slides down a 30-degree incline with acceleration g divided by 4. Along the slope: mg sin30° minus f equals mg divided by 4, so f equals mg divided by 4. Perpendicular: N equals mg times root 3 divided by 2. So µk equals f divided by N equals 1 divided by 2 root 3. <<TRACE:parallel-component>> The friction force from Newton's second law divided by the normal force from perpendicular equilibrium gives the kinetic coefficient directly. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mu_k = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> Here is a 2.5 kg block on a rough surface. It doesn't slide for forces less than 15 N, giving µs equals 15 divided by 2.5 times 10 equals 0.60. When pushed at 15 N, it slides 10 metres in 5 seconds — using s equals half a t squared, acceleration equals 0.8 metres per second squared. <<PAUSE:short>> With that acceleration, the net force equals 2.5 times 0.8 equals 2 N. Applied force minus friction equals 2 N, so kinetic friction equals 15 minus 2 equals 13 N. Therefore µk equals 13 divided by 25 equals 0.52. What if you push a block with a force angled toward the vertical — angle θ from vertical, friction coefficient µ? Horizontal: F sinθ equals µN. Vertical: N equals mg plus F cosθ. Solving: F equals µ mg divided by the quantity sine θ minus µ cosine θ. Combining the horizontal and vertical equilibrium equations eliminates N and gives the required push force as a function of the angle from the vertical. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F = \frac{\mu mg}{\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta}|id=eq-4|boxed>> If tan θ is less than µ, then sine θ minus µ cosine θ is negative, making F negative — physically impossible. This means if tangent of θ is less than µ, the block cannot be pushed no matter how large the force. The downward component grows friction faster than the sideways component overcomes it. <<FOCUS:incline-surface>> Block m hangs vertically beside block M on an incline of angle θ — friction µ at both contacts. For block m: tension T equals µ mg. For block M along the slope: T plus µ N2 equals Mg sinθ. This gives M divided by m equals µ divided by the quantity sine θ minus µ cosine θ. If tanθ is less than µ, the system stays at rest for any ratio M divided by m. For the block-A-B-C system where B hangs and A sits on C: acceleration a equals F divided by total mass M plus 2m. For block A: friction f equals µmg provides upward force to keep B stationary. Working through the limits gives minimum force F equals the quantity 1 minus µ over 1 plus µ times the quantity M plus 2m times g, and maximum force equals the quantity 1 plus µ over 1 minus µ times the quantity M plus 2m times g. <<FOCUS:block-on-incline>> Two blocks on a symmetric double incline — both at 45 degrees, M equals 2 kg, µs equals 0.28, µk equals 0.25. Minimum m equals 9 divided by 8 kg, maximum m equals 32 divided by 9 kg. If m is at minimum and gently pushed up, acceleration equals 0.31 metres per second squared. <<TRACE:block-on-incline>> Extended example one: a delivery driver tilts the back of a van to slide boxes down. The box starts sliding at 20 degrees. Using tan 20 degrees — about 0.36 — the driver now knows the friction coefficient between the box and the van floor without any special equipment. Extended example two: a 3 kg phone rests on a car dashboard. A horizontal push of 9 N is applied but the phone does not move. With g equals 10, normal force equals 30 N and friction force equals 9 N exactly. So µs is at least 9 divided by 30, which is 0.3 — useful for choosing dashboard materials. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> The big takeaway: tilt a surface and note the slipping angle — its tangent is µs. Reduce the angle until motion is uniform — that tangent is µk. Or hang weights on a pulley until a block just slides — hanger weight divided by block weight gives µs directly. Friction coefficients are not mysteries; they're just angles and weights in disguise. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about something that might surprise you — glass sliding on glass. When most people think of glass, they think of something smooth and slippery, like a window pane. So you might expect two glass surfaces rubbing together to have very low friction. But here is where things get really interesting, and a little counterintuitive. Glass surfaces, even ones that look perfectly smooth to the naked eye, are actually quite rough at the microscopic level. When you press two glass surfaces together, those tiny bumps and ridges interlock and grip each other, creating more friction than you might expect. In fact, glass on glass has a surprisingly high coefficient of friction compared to many other material pairs people assume are rougher. This is a great reminder that friction is not just about how something looks or feels to your fingers — it is about what is happening at a scale far too small for us to see directly. The smoothness you feel when you run your finger along glass is real at the scale of your fingertip, but at the microscopic scale, the surface is a landscape of peaks and valleys. Another fascinating thing about glass on glass is that if you press two very clean, very flat glass surfaces together with enough force, they can actually stick together quite strongly through a process related to molecular attraction. This is sometimes called cold welding or adhesion, and it shows that friction and sticking forces are deeply connected to the same underlying molecular forces. For now, the key takeaway is this — never assume that a material which looks smooth will have low friction. The actual friction between two surfaces depends on their microscopic structure, the forces pressing them together, and even the chemistry of the surfaces. Glass on glass is a perfect example of how our everyday intuitions about friction can lead us astray, and why physicists always look deeper than the surface.
topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:macro-glass-block-top>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:friction:0_04:glass_surfaces_diagram>> Glass feels perfectly smooth — so two glass surfaces rubbing together should slip easily, right? Actually, glass on glass grips harder than most people expect. Here's why. <<FOCUS:macro-glass-block-bottom>> Here are two glass blocks. topics.our_understanding: This section is titled Ice and ice, and it sits within a chapter on friction. The idea here is a fascinating one — what happens when you slide ice across ice? You might expect that because both surfaces are the same material, something special or unusual would happen, and you would be right to wonder about that. Ice on ice is actually a classic example used to illustrate how friction can be surprisingly low between two surfaces of the same kind, especially when that material has some unique properties. Ice is slippery, and when you put two icy surfaces together, the result is even less friction than you might get with many other material combinations. This connects to the broader story of friction, which is all about what happens at the boundary between two surfaces when one tries to slide over the other. The smoother and more similar the surfaces, the less they tend to grip each other — and ice, being naturally smooth and capable of forming a thin layer of liquid water under pressure or at its surface, is a perfect example of this principle in action. Understanding cases like ice on ice helps us appreciate that friction is not just one fixed thing — it changes depending on the materials involved, the conditions, and even the temperature. This is why ice rinks work, why hockey pucks glide so far, and why walking on ice feels so different from walking on pavement. Even though this section is brief, the concept it points to is genuinely important: the same physical laws of friction apply everywhere, but the numbers — how much friction actually exists — depend deeply on what the surfaces are made of and how they interact with each other.

topics.our_understanding:
Here is something that might surprise you — friction is not just about how rough or smooth a surface looks. It is also deeply affected by what is sitting on that surface at a microscopic level. Things like dust, tiny impurities, and a thin layer of oxidation — that is, the chemical reaction between a metal and oxygen in the air — actually play a huge role in determining how much friction exists between two objects.

Let me walk you through a fascinating experiment to make this concrete. Imagine you take two blocks of pure copper — not ordinary copper, but very carefully cleaned copper with no oxide layer, no dust, nothing on the surface at all. You also heat the blocks to drive out any gases that might be dissolved inside the metal. Then you place these two blocks in contact with each other inside a sealed chamber where almost all the air has been pumped out, so the pressure is extremely low.

What do you think happens? The two blocks actually stick together. They bond to each other. And when you try to slide one block over the other, you need a surprisingly large force to do it. In fact, the friction coefficient — which is normally a number less than one for most everyday materials — becomes much larger than one in this situation. That is extraordinary.

Why does this happen? When surfaces are perfectly clean and in very close contact, the atoms on one surface can actually interact directly with the atoms on the other surface. There is nothing in between to separate them. The surfaces essentially want to bond together, almost like they are becoming one piece of metal.

Now here is the really interesting part. If you let just a tiny amount of air back into that chamber, some oxidation happens — a thin chemical layer forms on the copper surfaces. And just like that, the friction coefficient drops back down to normal, everyday values. That thin oxide layer acts like a barrier between the two surfaces, preventing those direct atom-to-atom interactions.

This tells us something deep about friction. It is not just a mechanical phenomenon about bumps and grooves. It is also a chemical and atomic-level story. The invisible layers on surfaces — whether from oxidation, dust, or other impurities — are actually doing important work in keeping friction at the values we normally observe.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about something you encounter every single day — the grip between a rubber tyre and a wet concrete road. This is one of the most practically important friction situations in the real world, and understanding it could literally save lives. When a road is wet, a thin film of water gets between the tyre and the road surface. That water acts almost like a lubricant, reducing the contact between the rubber and the concrete. As a result, the friction force drops significantly compared to a dry road. Think about what that means for a car trying to stop quickly — with less friction available, the braking distance gets much longer. This is exactly why drivers are told to slow down in rainy conditions. The coefficient of friction, which is the number we use to describe how grippy two surfaces are against each other, is noticeably lower for rubber on wet concrete than for rubber on dry concrete. The coefficient of friction is just a ratio — it tells you how strong the friction force is compared to how hard the surfaces are being pushed together. A higher number means more grip, a lower number means less grip. Wet concrete gives you a lower number. Now, rubber is actually a fascinating material here. It is soft and flexible, so it can deform slightly and mould into the tiny bumps and grooves of a road surface. This is why rubber tyres grip better than, say, a hard plastic wheel would. But when water fills those tiny bumps and grooves, the rubber cannot make as much direct contact with the concrete, and that grip is reduced. Engineers who design tyres work very hard to cut grooves into the tyre tread — those patterns you see on a tyre — specifically to channel water away from the contact patch so the rubber can still touch the road even in wet conditions. So the value you see listed for rubber on wet concrete is a reminder that friction is not just about the two materials involved, but also about what is happening at the interface between them.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about something that might seem simple at first but is actually quite fascinating — friction between two surfaces made of the same material. Specifically, let's think about copper sliding against copper. You might expect that because both surfaces are identical, they would behave in a perfectly predictable, straightforward way. But here is where things get really interesting. When two copper surfaces are pressed together, the atoms on each surface are so similar that they can actually form temporary bonds with each other at the microscopic level. The surfaces are never perfectly smooth — even polished metal has tiny bumps and valleys when you zoom in close enough. These microscopic high points, called asperities, press into each other and can actually weld together momentarily. Because both surfaces are copper, the atoms recognize each other, so to speak, and these tiny cold welds form more readily than they would between two different materials. This means the friction between copper and copper can be surprisingly high — sometimes even higher than you might expect from a metal surface. Think about it this way: if you pressed two pieces of modeling clay together, they would stick because the material is the same and soft. Copper is harder, but at the microscopic scale, something similar happens. The coefficient of friction between copper and copper is notably significant, and engineers have to account for this when designing machines or systems where copper parts might rub against each other. This is also why lubrication is so important in engineering — adding a thin layer of oil or grease between two copper surfaces prevents those atomic bonds from forming and dramatically reduces friction. So the key insight here is that same-material contact does not mean low friction. In fact, material compatibility at the atomic level can make friction greater, not smaller. This is a wonderful reminder that friction is not just a surface-level phenomenon — it goes all the way down to the atomic scale.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about something you experience every single day without even thinking about it — the friction between a rubber tyre and a dry concrete road. The combination of a soft, grippy material like rubber and a rough surface like dry concrete gives us this impressively high friction value. This is why car tyres are made of rubber and not metal or plastic — engineers chose rubber precisely because of this high friction coefficient with road surfaces. Notice that the word dry is really important here. The moment water gets between the tyre and the road, that coefficient drops significantly, which is why wet roads are so much more dangerous. The 1.00 value is a benchmark — a clean, ideal case — and real-world conditions can change it quite a bit. topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about friction between two very common engineering materials: steel and brass. These two metals show up together all the time in machines, engines, and mechanical devices, so understanding how they interact through friction is really practical and important. When a steel surface slides against a brass surface, there is a specific frictional relationship between them that engineers have measured carefully over many years of experimentation. The coefficient of friction — which is the number that tells us how much frictional force exists compared to the normal force pushing the surfaces together — has a particular value for steel on brass that is different from, say, steel on steel or rubber on concrete. Think about why that matters: if you are designing a machine where a steel shaft spins inside a brass bearing, you need to know exactly how much friction you are dealing with so you can figure out how much energy is lost to heat, how much force is needed to keep things moving, and how long the parts will last before wearing out. The static coefficient of friction, which governs the force needed to get things moving from rest, is generally higher than the kinetic coefficient, which governs the force needed to keep things sliding once they are already in motion. This is true for steel and brass just as it is for most material pairs. Brass is often chosen as a bearing material precisely because it has a relatively low coefficient of friction with steel, meaning less energy is wasted and less heat is generated in the contact zone. This is a great example of how the physics of friction directly influences real engineering decisions. Even though this section is brief, the underlying idea is powerful: the materials you choose determine the friction you get, and friction determines how well your machine works.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something you experience every single day without even thinking about it — friction. But before we get to friction specifically, we need to understand where it comes from. When two objects touch each other, the tiny charged particles on their surfaces interact through electromagnetic forces. These interactions add up to produce what we call a contact force — one object pushing on the other. And notice, by Newton's third law, the two objects push on each other with equal strength but in opposite directions.

Now here's the key insight of this section. That contact force doesn't have to point straight into the surface. It can point at an angle. So we do something very useful — we split it into two parts, or components. One part points perpendicular to the surface, meaning straight into or away from it. We call that the normal force. The other part runs parallel to the surface, meaning along it. That parallel component is what we call friction.

Think about a book resting on a table. The table pushes back on the book. If the book is just sitting still, that push is straight up — all normal force, no friction. But the moment you try to slide the book and the table resists, that resistance is friction — the parallel part of the contact force.

Now, friction comes in two flavors. When two surfaces are actually sliding over each other, we call it kinetic friction. When they're in contact but not sliding — like a book you're pressing against a wall — we call it static friction. Both are just the parallel component of that contact force, but they behave a little differently, and we'll explore that more as we go.

Also worth knowing — friction isn't only between solids. It can act between a solid and a fluid, or between two fluids. When fluids are involved, we call it viscous force. But for now, we're focusing on solid surfaces rubbing against each other.

The beautiful thing here is that even though the microscopic electromagnetic interactions are incredibly complicated, we can describe friction's behavior with just a few simple laws. That's the power of physics — finding simple patterns in complex situations.

When two bodies in contact move with respect to

The kinetic friction on a body A slipping against

It should be carefully noted that the velocity

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about kinetic friction — the kind of friction that shows up when two surfaces are already sliding against each other. The word 'kinetic' just means moving, so kinetic friction is friction in motion. Whenever two objects rub past each other, each one experiences a friction force that tries to slow down that relative sliding. The key word there is 'relative' — and we'll come back to that in a moment because it's where students often get confused.

First, let's think about direction. The rule is this: the kinetic friction on an object acts opposite to the direction that object is moving relative to the surface it's sliding on. Notice it's not just 'opposite to motion' in general — it's opposite to the motion as seen from the other surface. Here's a great example to make that concrete. Imagine a wheeled box rolling to the right on a road, and a small block sitting on top of that box. The block is also moving right as seen from the road, but it's moving slower than the box. So from the box's point of view, the block is sliding backward — toward the left. That means the friction the box exerts on the block points to the right, trying to drag the block along. And by Newton's third law, the block pushes back on the box with friction pointing to the left. Same situation, two different friction directions — because direction always depends on whose perspective you're taking.

Now let's talk about magnitude. The kinetic friction force equals the coefficient of kinetic friction multiplied by the normal force between the two surfaces. The coefficient, which we call mu-k, is just a number that tells you how rough or smooth the surfaces are. Smooth surfaces have a small mu-k, rough surfaces have a large one. Two really important things fall out of this relationship. First, the friction force does not depend on how fast the objects are sliding — once they're moving, the friction stays constant at mu-k times the normal force, regardless of speed. This holds well for everyday speeds. Second, and this surprises many students, the friction force does not depend on the area of contact. A wide flat slab and the same slab standing on its narrow edge experience the same friction force on the same table, as long as the weight pressing down is the same. That's a genuinely counterintuitive result, and it comes directly from the formula.

6.3 STATIC FRICTION
Frictional forces can also act between two bodies
which are in contact but are not sliding with respect
to each other. The friction in such cases is called static
friction. For example, suppose several labourers are
trying to push a heavy almirah on the floor to take it
out of a room (figure 6.7).
The almirah is heavy and even the most sincere
effort by them is not able to slide it on the floor even
by a millimeter. As the almirah is at rest the resultant
force on the almirah should be zero. Thus, something
is exerting a force on the almirah in the opposite
direction. In this case, it is the floor which exerts a
frictional force on the almirah. The labourers push the
almirah towards left in figure (6.7) and the floor exerts
a frictional force on the almirah towards right. This is
an example of static friction.
How strong is this frictional force ? Suppose the
almirah is pushed with a small force in the beginning
and the force is gradually increased. It does not slide
until the force applied is greater than a minimum
value say F. The force of static friction is equal and
opposite to the force exerted by the labourers as long
as the almirah is at rest. This means that the
magnitude of static friction adjusts its value according
to the applied force. As the applied force increases, the
frictional force also increases. The static friction is
thus, self adjustable. It adjusts its magnitude (and
direction) in such a way that together with other forces
applied on the body, it maintains ‘relative rest’
between the two surfaces. However, the frictional force
cannot go beyond a maximum. When the applied force
exceeds this maximum, friction fails to increase its
value and slipping starts. The maximum static friction
that a body can exert on the other body in contact with
it, is called limiting friction. This limiting friction is
proportional to the normal contact force between the
two bodies. We can write
             fmax = µs N
… (6.2)
where fmax is the maximum possible force of static
friction and N  is the normal force. The constant of
proportionality is called the coefficient of static friction
and its value again depends on the material and
roughness of the two surfaces in contact. In general,
µs is slightly greater than µk . As long as the normal
force is constant, the maximum possible friction does
not depend on the area of the surfaces in contact.
Once again we emphasise that µs N  is the
maximum possible force of static friction that can act
between the bodies. The actual force of static friction
may be smaller than µs N  and its value depends on
other forces acting on the body. The magnitude of
frictional force is equal to that required to keep the
body at relative rest. Thus,

Finding the Direction of Static Friction
The direction of static friction on a body is such
that the total force acting on it keeps it at rest with
respect to the body in contact. Newton’s first or second
law can often be used to find the direction of static
friction. Figure (6.9) shows a block A placed on another

The block B is pulled by a force F towards right.
Suppose the force is small and the blocks do not move.
Let us focus our attention on the upper block. The
upper block is at rest with respect to the ground which
is assumed to be inertial. Thus, the resultant force on
the upper block is zero (Newton’s first law). As no other
external force acts on the upper block the friction
acting on the upper block due to the lower block, must
be zero. If the force F is increased, the two blocks move
together towards right, with some acceleration. As the
upper block accelerates towards right the resultant
force on it must be towards right. As friction is the
only horizontal force on the upper block it must be
towards right.
Notice that it is the friction on the upper block
which accelerates it towards right. It is a general
misconception that friction always opposes the motion.
It is not really true. In many cases friction causes the
motion. A vehicle accelerates on the road only because
the frictional force on the vehicle due to the road drives
it. It is not possible to accelerate a vehicle on a
frictionless road. Friction opposes the relative motion
between the bodies in contact.
Another way to find the direction of static friction
is as follows. For a moment consider the surfaces to
be frictionless. In absence of friction the bodies will
start slipping against each other. One should then find
the direction of friction as opposite to the velocity with
respect to the body applying the friction.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about static friction — the kind of friction that acts when two surfaces are touching but not sliding against each other. Think about a really heavy wardrobe sitting on a floor. A group of workers push hard against it, but it doesn't budge even a tiny bit. Now, if the wardrobe isn't moving, Newton's first law tells us the net force on it must be zero. The workers are pushing it one way, so something must be pushing back the other way with exactly the same strength. That something is static friction from the floor.

Here's what makes static friction really interesting — it's self-adjusting. If the workers push gently, the friction is small. If they push harder, the friction gets bigger to match. It always does exactly what's needed to keep the object still. But there's a limit. Push hard enough, and the friction can't keep up anymore. The object starts to slide. That maximum value of static friction is called limiting friction.

We can express limiting friction in words like this: the maximum static friction force equals the coefficient of static friction multiplied by the normal force pressing the two surfaces together. The coefficient of static friction, which we call mu-s, is a number that depends on what the two surfaces are made of and how rough they are. Importantly, mu-s is usually a little bit larger than the kinetic friction coefficient, meaning it's harder to get something moving than to keep it moving once it already is.

One thing to be really careful about: the formula gives you the maximum possible static friction, not the actual friction at every moment. The actual static friction could be anything from zero up to that maximum, depending on what other forces are acting.

Now, finding the direction of static friction is something students often get wrong. A common mistake is thinking friction always opposes motion. That's not quite right — friction opposes relative motion between surfaces. In fact, friction can actually cause motion. When a car accelerates forward, it's the friction from the road pushing the car forward that makes it speed up. Without friction, the wheels would just spin in place and the car would go nowhere. A helpful trick for finding the direction of static friction is to imagine for a moment that the surfaces are frictionless. Ask yourself: which way would the object start to slip? Static friction acts in the opposite direction to that imagined slip.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about the laws of friction — the rules that govern how friction behaves between any two surfaces in contact. These laws are beautifully simple, and once you understand them, you can predict how objects will move in almost any real-world situation.

First, think about what happens when two objects are already sliding against each other. In that case, we call the friction kinetic friction, and it equals the coefficient of kinetic friction multiplied by the normal force. The normal force is just how hard the two surfaces are pressing against each other. The coefficient of kinetic friction is a number — usually between zero and one — that tells you how 'grippy' those two particular surfaces are together. Steel on ice has a very low coefficient, while rubber on rough concrete has a much higher one.

Now, the direction of kinetic friction is always opposite to the direction the object is moving relative to the surface it's sliding on. So if a box is sliding to the right across a floor, kinetic friction pushes it to the left. That makes intuitive sense — friction resists the motion.

The third law covers static friction, which is what acts when the two surfaces are NOT sliding. Here's the key insight: static friction is not a fixed value. It adjusts itself to whatever is needed to prevent slipping, up to a maximum limit. That maximum is the coefficient of static friction multiplied by the normal force. So static friction can be anywhere from zero up to that maximum. This is why you can push gently on a heavy box and it stays still — static friction matches your push exactly. Push harder and harder, and eventually you exceed that maximum, and the box starts to slide.

The fourth law is perhaps the most surprising one: friction does not depend on the area of contact, as long as the normal force stays the same. A wide flat box and a narrow tall box with the same weight will experience the same friction. This seems strange at first, but it's a well-established experimental result.

Finally, notice that the actual values of these friction coefficients depend on the specific materials involved and how smooth or rough their surfaces are. A table of typical values gives you a rough guide, but real-world conditions like moisture, temperature, and surface preparation can all change things. The key takeaway is that friction is predictable, rule-based, and something you can calculate — which makes it a powerful tool in physics.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what friction actually is at the deepest level — not just a force that slows things down, but something rooted in the tiny world of atoms and molecules. This is one of those beautiful moments in physics where zooming in completely changes how you see something familiar.

Imagine you have a steel plate that looks perfectly smooth and shiny. You run your finger across it and it feels flat. But if you could shrink down and look at that surface with an incredibly powerful microscope, you would see something surprising — hills, valleys, bumps, and craters everywhere. Every surface, no matter how polished it looks to your eye, is actually quite rough at the atomic scale. Think of it like a mountain range that looks flat from an airplane but is full of peaks and cliffs when you're standing on the ground.

Now, when you place two objects on top of each other, those rough atomic surfaces don't touch everywhere. Only the tips of the tiny bumps on one surface actually touch the tips of the bumps on the other surface. This means the real area where the two objects are actually in contact is much, much smaller than the total surface area you can see. It's like two crumpled pieces of foil pressed together — they only touch at a few high points.

At those tiny contact points, the atoms of the two surfaces are so close together that molecular forces kick in. The particles from each surface attract each other and form what we call molecular bonds — tiny connections between the two materials right at those contact spots.

Here's where it gets really interesting. When you try to slide one object over the other, you have to break all those little molecular bonds. Breaking them takes energy and requires a force. But it doesn't stop there — as the bonds break, the material around them gets slightly deformed and disturbed. That disturbance travels through the object as tiny vibration waves. Over time, those vibrations die out, and the energy from them gets converted into random motion of the particles inside the object. Random particle motion is exactly what we mean by heat. So the objects actually warm up! This is why your hands get warm when you rub them together, and why a drill bit gets hot when it cuts through wood.

New bonds also keep forming as the surfaces slide, which means you need a continuous force just to keep the motion going. This is the atomic story of friction — bond breaking, deformation, vibrations, and heat, all happening at a scale too small to see but with effects large enough to feel every single day.

topics.our_understanding:
Today we are going to look at two clever laboratory methods physicists use to actually measure friction coefficients — not just talk about them in theory, but get real numbers from real experiments.

The first method uses a horizontal table. Imagine a wooden block sitting on a plank. A string connects the block, runs over a frictionless pulley at the edge, and hangs down to a weight hanger. You keep adding weights to the hanger until the block just barely starts to slide. At that magic moment, the tension pulling the block equals the weight hanging on the hanger, and that tension is exactly the maximum static friction force. The normal force holding the block up equals the block's own weight since everything is level. So the coefficient of static friction is simply the hanger weight divided by the block weight. To find kinetic friction, you reduce the hanging weight slightly and give the block a gentle push. You adjust until the block glides at perfectly steady speed — no speeding up, no slowing down. At constant velocity, the net force is zero, so the tension again equals the kinetic friction force. Divide that new hanger weight by the block weight and you have the kinetic friction coefficient. You can also verify something important here: if you stack extra weights on the block, the friction force goes up, but when you divide by the new larger normal force, you get the same coefficient. And if you flip the block onto a different face, changing the contact area, the coefficient stays the same too. These are beautiful experimental confirmations of the laws of friction.

The second method uses an inclined plank — no pulley needed. You tilt the plank gradually until the block just starts to slip. At that critical angle, the component of gravity pulling the block down the slope exactly equals the maximum static friction pushing back up. When you work through the geometry, the coefficient of static friction turns out to equal the tangent of that angle, which you can calculate just by measuring the height and horizontal distance of the plank — tangent equals height divided by horizontal distance. For kinetic friction, you reduce the angle slightly and push the block to get it moving, then adjust until it moves at constant speed. Again, the kinetic friction coefficient equals the tangent of that new angle. This method is wonderfully simple because you only need a ruler, not a set of hanging weights.

We also briefly meet rolling friction here. When a wheel rolls without sliding, the contact point is momentarily at rest relative to the ground, so there is no kinetic rubbing. Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings are so useful in machines — they dramatically cut down energy loss.

1. The coefficient of static friction between a block of mass m and an incline is µs = 0.3. (a) What can be the maximum angle θ of the incline with the horizontal so that the block does not slip on the plane ? (b) If the incline makes an angle θ/2 with the horizontal, find the frictional force on the block.
Solution : (a) the forces on the block are (i) the weight mg downward by the earth, (ii) the normal contact force N by the incline, and (iii) the friction f parallel to the incline up the plane, by the incline. As the block is at rest, these forces should add up to zero. Also, since θ is the maximum angle to prevent slipping, this is a case of limiting equilibrium and so f = µs N.
Taking components perpendicular to the incline,
N − mg cosθ = 0
or, N = mg cosθ. … (i)
Taking components parallel to the incline,
f − mg sinθ = 0
or, f = mg sinθ
or, µs N = mg sinθ. … (ii)
Dividing (ii) by (i) µs = tanθ
or, θ = tan−1 µs = tan−1 (0.3).
(b) If the angle of incline is reduced to θ/2, the equilibrium is not limiting, and hence the force of static friction f is less than µs N. To know the value of f, we proceed as in part (a) and get the equations
N = mg cos(θ/2)
and f = mg sin(θ/2).
Thus, the force of friction is mg sin(θ/2).

2. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to a block of mass 4 kg resting on a rough horizontal table. If the block does not move on the table, how much frictional force the table is applying on the block ? What can be said about the coefficient of static friction between the block and the table ? Take g = 10 m/s2.
Solution : The forces on the block are (a) 4 kg × 10 m/s2 = 40 N downward by the earth, (b) N upward by the table, (c) 20 N towards right by the experimenter and (d) f towards left by the table (friction). As the block is at rest, these forces should add up to zero. Taking horizontal and vertical components,
f = 20 N and N = 40 N.
Thus, the table exerts a frictional (static) force of 20 N on the block in the direction opposite to the applied force. Since it is a case of static friction,
f ≤ µs N, or, µs ≥ f/N or, µs ≥ 0.5.
book_examples.lesson_focus: When a block remains stationary under an applied force, the static friction exactly cancels that force, and you can find a lower bound for the friction coefficient from the ratio of friction force to normal force.

Solution : Consider the equilibrium of the block of mass m. The forces on this block are (a) mg downward by the earth and (b) T upward by the string.
Hence, T − mg = 0 or, T = mg. … (i)
Now consider the equilibrium of the 2 kg block. The forces on this block are (a) T towards right by the string, (b) f towards left (friction) by the table, (c) 20 N downward (weight) by the earth and (d) N upward (normal force) by the table.
For vertical equilibrium of this block,
N = 20 N. … (ii)
As m is the largest mass which can be used without moving the system, the friction is limiting.
Thus, f = µs N. … (iii)
For horizontal equilibrium of the 2 kg block,
f = T. … (iv)
Using equations (i), (iii) and (iv)
µs N = mg
or, 0.2 × 20 N = mg
or, m = 0.2 × 20 / 10 kg = 0.4 kg.

4. The coefficient of static friction between the two blocks shown in figure (6-W4) is µ and the table is smooth. What maximum horizontal force F can be applied to the block of mass M so that the blocks move together ?
Solution : When the maximum force F is applied, both the blocks move together towards right. The only horizontal force on the upper block of mass m is that due to the friction by the lower block of mass M. Hence this force on m should be towards right. The force of friction on M by m should be towards left by Newton's third law. As we are talking of the maximum possible force F that can be applied, the friction is limiting and hence f = µ N, where N is the normal force between the blocks.
Consider the motion of m. The forces on m are, (a) mg downward by the earth (gravity), (b) N upward by the block M (normal force) and (c) f = µ N (friction) towards right by the block M.
In the vertical direction, there is no acceleration. This gives
N = mg. … (i)
In the horizontal direction, let the acceleration be a, then
µ N = m a
or, µ mg = ma
or, a = µ g. … (ii)
Next, consider the motion of M. The equation of motion is
F − µ N = M a
or, F − µ mg = M µ g [Using (i) and (ii)]
or, F = µ g (M + m).

5. A block slides down an incline of angle 30° with an acceleration g/4. Find the kinetic friction coefficient.
Solution : Let the mass of the block be m. The forces on the block are, (a) mg downward by the earth (gravity), (b) N normal force by the incline and (c) f up the plane, (friction) by the incline.
Taking components parallel to the incline and writing Newton's second law,
mg sin 30° − f = mg/4
or, f = mg/4.
There is no acceleration perpendicular to the incline. Hence,
N = mg cos 30° = mg · √3/2.
As the block is slipping on the incline, friction is f = µk N.
So, µk = f/N = (mg/4) / (mg√3/2) = 1/(2√3).

6. A block of mass 2.5 kg is kept on a rough horizontal surface. It is found that the block does not slide if a horizontal force less than 15 N is applied to it. Also it is found that it takes 5 seconds to slide through the first 10 m if a horizontal force of 15 N is applied and the block is gently pushed to start the motion. Taking g = 10 m/s2, calculate the coefficients of static and kinetic friction between the block and the surface.
Solution : The forces acting on the block are shown in figure (6-W8). Here M = 2.5 kg and F = 15 N.
When F = 15 N is applied to the block, the block remains in limiting equilibrium. The force of friction is thus f = µs N. Applying Newton's first law,
f = µs N and N = mg
so that F = µs Mg
or, µs = F/mg = 15 N / ((2.5 kg)(10 m/s2)) = 0.60.
When the block is gently pushed to start the motion, kinetic friction acts between the block and the surface. Since the block takes 5 second to slide through the first 10 m, the acceleration a is given by
10 m = (1/2) a (5 s)2
or, a = 20/25 m/s2 = 0.8 m/s2.
The frictional force is
f = µk N = µk Mg.
Applying Newton's second law
F − µk Mg = Ma
or, µk = (F − Ma) / Mg
= (15 N − (2.5 kg)(0.8 m/s2)) / ((2.5 kg)(10 m/s2))
= 0.52.

book_examples.verbatim_text:
7. A block placed on a horizontal surface is being pushed by a force F making an angle θ with the vertical. If the friction coefficient is µ, how much force is needed to get the block just started. Discuss the situation when tanθ < µ.
Solution : The situation is shown in figure (6-W9). In the limiting equilibrium the frictional force f will be equal to µ N. For horizontal equilibrium
F sinθ = µ N
For vertical equilibrium
F cosθ + mg = N.
Eliminating N from these equations,
F sinθ = µ F cosθ + µ mg
or, F = µ mg / (sinθ − µ cosθ).
If tanθ < µ we have (sinθ − µ cosθ) < 0 and then F is negative. So for angles less than tan−1 µ, one cannot push the block ahead, however large the force may be.
book_examples.lesson_focus: When pushing a block with a force angled toward the vertical, there is a critical angle below which no amount of force can slide the block because the downward component increases friction faster than the horizontal component overcomes it.

Friction coefficient is µ

book_examples.verbatim_text:
8. Find the maximum value of M/m in the situation shown in figure (6-W10) so that the system remains at rest. Friction coefficient at both the contacts is µ. Discuss the situation when tanθ < µ.
Solution : Equilibrium of the block m gives
T = µ N1 and N1 = mg
which gives
T = µ mg. … (i)
Next, consider the equilibrium of the block M. Taking components parallel to the incline
T + µ N2 = Mg sinθ.
Taking components normal to the incline
N2 = Mg cosθ.
These give T = Mg (sinθ − µ cosθ). … (ii)
From (i) and (ii), µ mg = Mg (sinθ − µ cosθ)
or, M/m = µ / (sinθ − µ cosθ)
If tanθ < µ, (sinθ − µ cosθ) < 0 and the system will not slide for any value of M/m.
book_examples.lesson_focus: The maximum ratio of masses in a block-on-incline pulley system at rest is set by balancing the tension from the hanging block against the net force along the incline on the other block.

Block m hangs vertically, block M is on the incline at angle θ
Tension T equals µ times mg
