book_examples.verbatim_text:
9. Consider the situation shown in figure (6-W12). The horizontal surface below the bigger block is smooth. The coefficient of friction between the blocks is µ. Find the minimum and the maximum force F that can be applied in order to keep the smaller block at rest with respect to the bigger block.
Solution : If no force is applied, the block A will slip on C towards right and the block B will move downward. Suppose the minimum force needed to prevent slipping is F. Taking A + B + C as the system, the only external horizontal force on the system is F. Hence the acceleration of the system is
a = F / (M + 2m). … (i)
Now take the block A as the system. For vertical equilibrium N = mg. As the minimum force needed to prevent slipping is applied, the friction is limiting. Thus,
f = µ N = µ mg.
As the block moves towards right with an acceleration a,
T − f = ma
or, T − µ mg = ma. … (ii)
Now take the block B as the system. As the block moves towards right with an acceleration a,
N′ = ma.
As the friction is limiting, f′ = µ N′ = µ ma.
For vertical equilibrium
T + f′ = mg
or, T + µ ma = mg. … (iii)
Eliminating T from (ii) and (iii)
amin = ((1 − µ)/(1 + µ)) g.
When a large force is applied the block A slips on C towards left and the block B slips on C in the upward direction. The friction on A is towards right and that on B is downwards. Solving as above, the acceleration in this case is
amax = ((1 + µ)/(1 − µ)) g.
Thus, a lies between ((1 − µ)/(1 + µ)) g and ((1 + µ)/(1 − µ)) g.
From (i) the force F should be between
((1 − µ)/(1 + µ)) (M + 2m) g and ((1 + µ)/(1 − µ)) (M + 2m) g.

Total system mass is M plus 2m
Minimum acceleration is quantity 1 minus µ divided by 1 plus µ times g
Maximum acceleration is quantity 1 plus µ divided by 1 minus µ times g
Minimum force F is quantity 1 minus µ divided by 1 plus µ times quantity M plus 2m times g

10. Figure (6-W15) shows two blocks connected by a light string placed on the two inclined parts of a triangular structure. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction are 0.28 and 0.25 respectively at each of the surfaces. (a) Find the minimum and maximum values of m for which the system remains at rest. (b) Find the acceleration of either block if m is given the minimum value calculated in the first part and is gently pushed up the incline for a short while.
Solution : (a) Take the 2 kg block as the system. It is assumed that m has its minimum value so that the 2 kg block has a tendency to slip down.
Taking components perpendicular to the incline
N = Mg cos 45° = Mg/√2.
Taking components parallel to the incline
T + f = Mg sin 45° = Mg/√2
or, T = Mg/√2 − f.
As it is a case of limiting equilibrium,
f = µs N
or, T = (Mg/√2)(1 − µs). … (i)
For the block of mass m:
N′ = mg cos 45° = mg/√2.
T = mg sin 45° + f′ = mg/√2 + f′.
f′ = µs N′ = µs mg/√2.
Thus, T = (mg/√2)(1 + µs). … (ii)
From (i) and (ii)
m(1 + µs) = M(1 − µs) … (iii)
or, m = ((1 − µs)/(1 + µs)) M = ((1 − 0.28)/(1 + 0.28)) × 2 kg = 9/8 kg.
When maximum possible value of m is supplied, the directions of friction are reversed. Thus, the maximum value of m is
m = ((1 + 0.28)/(1 − 0.28)) × 2 kg = 32/9 kg.
(b) If m = 9/8 kg and the system is gently pushed, kinetic friction will operate. µk = 0.25.
For M: Mg sin 45° − T − f = Ma
or, (Mg/√2) − T − µk(Mg/√2) = Ma. … (iv)
For m: T − mg sin 45° − f′ = ma
or, T − mg/√2 − µk(mg/√2) = ma. … (v)
Adding (iv) and (v):
(Mg/√2)(1 − µk) − (mg/√2)(1 + µk) = (M + m)a
or, a = [M(1 − µk) − m(1 + µk)] g / [√2(M + m)]
= [2 × 0.75 − (9/8) × 1.25] / [√2(2 + 9/8)] g
= 0.31 m/s2.

questions.q_text: A 50-newton box sits on a flat floor. You push it horizontally with 20 newtons, but it doesn't move. What is the magnitude of the static friction force acting on the box at that moment?
options: A. 0 newtons, because the box isn't moving
B. 50 newtons, because that equals the weight of the box
C. 20 newtons, because friction adjusts to match the applied force
D. More than 20 newtons, because static friction always exceeds the applied force

questions.q_text: The coefficient of static friction between a crate and a floor is 0.4, and the normal force on the crate is 200 newtons. A horizontal push of 60 newtons is applied and the crate does not move. Which statement is correct?
options: A. The static friction force is 80 newtons, because that is what the formula gives
B. The static friction force is 60 newtons, because the crate is stationary and friction self-adjusts
C. The static friction force is 80 newtons only if the crate is on the verge of slipping
D. The static friction force cannot be determined without knowing the kinetic friction coefficient

questions.q_text: A wooden crate weighing 300 newtons rests on a concrete floor. The coefficient of static friction between wood and concrete is 0.5. A worker pushes the crate horizontally. What is the minimum horizontal force needed to just start the crate moving, and what is the actual static friction force when the worker is pushing with only 100 newtons?
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Find the normal force. Since the crate is on a flat floor and not accelerating vertically, the normal force equals the weight of the crate: normal force = 300 newtons.

Step 2 — Find the maximum (limiting) static friction. Limiting friction = coefficient of static friction multiplied by normal force = 0.5 multiplied by 300 = 150 newtons. This is the maximum friction the floor can provide.

Step 3 — Minimum force to start movement. The crate will just begin to move when the applied force exceeds the limiting friction. So the worker must apply just over 150 newtons to start the crate sliding. The minimum force to initiate motion is 150 newtons.

Step 4 — Actual static friction at 100 newtons push. Since 100 newtons is less than the 150-newton limit, the crate stays still. By Newton's first law, the net force must be zero, so static friction self-adjusts to exactly 100 newtons — not 150 newtons. The formula only gives the maximum possible value, not the value at every moment.

questions.q_text: A heavy box is sitting still on a rough floor. Once a worker finally gets it moving, she notices it becomes easier to keep pushing it than it was to get it started. Which principle best explains this observation?
options: A. The normal force decreases once the box is in motion
B. The coefficient of static friction is greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction, so the maximum resisting force before motion exceeds the friction force during motion
C. Static friction disappears entirely once the box moves, so there is no resistance at all
D. The worker's muscles warm up, making her stronger after the initial push

questions.q_text: A person stands on the floor of a bus that suddenly accelerates forward. Imagining for a moment that the floor were frictionless, which way would the person's feet tend to slip relative to the bus floor — and therefore, which direction does static friction actually push the person?

B. Feet slip backward, so friction pushes the person forward
C. Feet slip backward, so friction pushes the person backward

questions.q_text: Glass surfaces feel smooth to the touch, yet glass sliding on glass has a surprisingly high coefficient of friction. What is the main reason for this?
options: A. Glass is a liquid at room temperature, so its surface flows and grips other surfaces.
B. At the microscopic level, glass surfaces have peaks and valleys that interlock and grip each other.
C. Glass is electrically charged, which creates magnetic attraction between the two surfaces.
D. The weight of glass is unusually high, which automatically increases friction.

questions.q_text: A physics student is given four pairs of materials and asked to rank them from highest to lowest friction based only on how smooth they look. She ranks glass on glass as the lowest because it looks the smoothest. Explain why this ranking is likely wrong, and describe what she should consider instead to make a better prediction.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Identify the flaw in her reasoning. The student is using visible smoothness as her only guide. This is unreliable because friction is determined by what happens at the microscopic scale, not at the scale visible to the naked eye or felt by a fingertip. Step 2 — Explain what is actually happening with glass on glass. Even though glass looks and feels smooth, its surface at the microscopic level is covered in tiny peaks and valleys. When two glass surfaces are pressed together, these microscopic features interlock and grip each other, producing a surprisingly high coefficient of friction. Step 3 — Identify what she should consider instead. A better prediction requires thinking about three things: the microscopic surface structure of each material pair, the normal force pressing the surfaces together, and the surface chemistry. Simply looking at a material and judging its smoothness by eye is not sufficient. Step 4 — Conclusion. Glass on glass should not automatically be ranked lowest in friction. In fact, it may rank higher than material pairs that look rougher to the eye. The student's ranking is likely wrong because she is letting everyday intuition override the physics of what happens at scales too small to see directly.

questions.q_text: In the rolling-box example from the lesson, kinetic friction from the box acts on the block pointing to the right. By Newton's third law, what is the reaction force, and in which direction does it point?

questions.q_text: A 20 kilogram suitcase is being dragged horizontally across an airport floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the suitcase and the floor is 0.35. Taking gravitational acceleration as 10 metres per second squared, calculate the kinetic friction force acting on the suitcase. Then explain what would happen to that friction force if the suitcase were dragged twice as fast.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Find the normal force. Because the suitcase moves horizontally and there is no vertical acceleration, the normal force equals the weight of the suitcase. Weight equals mass times g, so normal force equals 20 kg times 10 m per second squared, which gives 200 newtons.

Step 2 — Apply the kinetic friction formula. Kinetic friction equals mu-k times the normal force, so friction equals 0.35 times 200 newtons, which equals 70 newtons.

Step 3 — Address the speed question. The kinetic friction formula depends only on mu-k and the normal force — neither of which changes when the speed doubles. Therefore the friction force remains exactly 70 newtons even at twice the speed. This is a key property of kinetic friction: it is independent of sliding speed.

questions.q_text: A steel block weighing 200 newtons rests on a flat brass surface. The static coefficient of friction between steel and brass is 0.35. What is the minimum horizontal force needed to start the block sliding? Once it is moving, the kinetic coefficient is 0.25. What force is required to keep it sliding at constant speed?
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the normal force. Since the block rests on a horizontal surface and is not accelerating vertically, the normal force equals the weight: N = 200 newtons.

Step 2 — Calculate the maximum static friction force. Friction force (static) = static coefficient times normal force = 0.35 times 200 = 70 newtons. This is the force that must be overcome to start motion, so the minimum force needed to begin sliding is 70 newtons.

Step 3 — Calculate the kinetic friction force. Friction force (kinetic) = kinetic coefficient times normal force = 0.25 times 200 = 50 newtons. To keep the block moving at constant speed, you must apply exactly 50 newtons horizontally, balancing the kinetic friction force.

Conclusion: 70 newtons to start motion; 50 newtons to maintain constant sliding. Notice that the force required drops once motion begins, which is the practical consequence of the static coefficient being higher than the kinetic coefficient.

questions.q_text: The coefficient of friction between steel and brass is described as a number that compares frictional force to normal force. If this coefficient is 0.30 and the normal force is 500 newtons, what does that tell you about the frictional force?

questions.q_text: A hockey puck slides across an ice rink. Explain, using the concept of ice on ice friction, why the puck travels such a long distance before stopping, and what would happen if the same puck were slid across a dry wooden floor instead.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Identify the surfaces in each case. On the ice rink, the puck's bottom surface (also very smooth and cold) is sliding over ice. This is essentially a case of very smooth surfaces interacting, and ice can form a thin liquid water layer at its surface, which acts almost like a lubricant. Step 2 — Explain the low friction on ice. Because both surfaces are smooth and the liquid water layer reduces the grip between them, the frictional force opposing the puck's motion is very small. A small frictional force means the puck decelerates slowly, so it travels a long distance before stopping. Step 3 — Contrast with a wooden floor. Wood is a much rougher surface at the microscopic level compared to ice. There is no liquid layer forming between the puck and the wood. The irregularities of the wood surface grip the puck's bottom, creating a much larger frictional force. Step 4 — Conclusion. On the wooden floor, the larger friction force decelerates the puck much more quickly, so it stops in a much shorter distance. This comparison shows clearly that friction is not fixed — it depends strongly on what the surfaces are made of and their physical properties.

questions.q_text: A student claims that friction between two surfaces is always the same fixed value no matter what the surfaces are made of. Based on the concept of ice on ice, which response best challenges this claim?

questions.q_text: In the horizontal table method, a block weighing 5 newtons just starts to slide when the hanging weight reaches 2 newtons. What is the coefficient of static friction?

questions.q_text: A block is placed on an inclined plank. The plank is slowly raised until the block just begins to slip. At that moment, the height of the raised end is 30 centimetres and the horizontal distance along the base is 50 centimetres. Calculate the coefficient of static friction.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall that for the inclined plane method, the coefficient of static friction equals the tangent of the critical angle at which the block just starts to slip. Step 2: Tangent of the angle equals height divided by horizontal distance. Step 3: Tangent = 30 divided by 50 = 0.6. Step 4: Therefore, the coefficient of static friction is 0.6.

questions.q_text: An engineer is designing a machine where two copper components will repeatedly slide against each other. Based on the principles of copper-on-copper friction, what is the most important design consideration the engineer should address?

questions.q_text: A student claims that a perfectly polished copper surface pressed against another perfectly polished copper surface would have very low friction because there are no bumps to catch on each other. Using what you know about asperities and atomic bonding, explain why this reasoning is flawed.
questions.answer: The student's reasoning contains two errors. First, no surface is truly perfectly smooth at the atomic scale — even the most carefully polished metal still has microscopic bumps and valleys called asperities when examined closely enough. These asperities on both surfaces press into each other when the surfaces are in contact. Second, and more importantly, even if the surfaces were extremely smooth, that would actually make things worse, not better. Smoother surfaces bring more atoms into close contact across a larger area, which means more opportunities for temporary atomic bonds to form. Because both surfaces are copper, the atoms on each side are chemically identical and bond with each other readily — a process called cold welding. So a highly polished copper-on-copper contact could actually produce more friction, not less, because the increased contact area allows even more of these atomic bonds to form. The student has confused macroscopic smoothness with low friction, ignoring the atomic-scale interactions that drive friction in same-material contacts.

questions.q_text: An engineer is designing a precision mechanism that will operate in outer space, where there is effectively no atmosphere. She uses two steel components that have been carefully cleaned and polished to remove all surface contamination. After assembly in the vacuum of space, she finds the components are extremely difficult to move against each other — far more so than ground tests predicted. Using what you know about surface impurities and friction, explain why this happened and what she could do to prevent it.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the problem: On Earth during ground tests, the steel surfaces had thin oxide layers and traces of dust or other contaminants on them. These invisible layers acted as barriers between the two surfaces, keeping friction at normal, manageable levels.

Step 2 — Explain what changed in space: In the vacuum of space, there is no oxygen or air to maintain or reform those oxide layers. After careful cleaning, the surfaces are essentially pure metal with no barrier between them. When the components are pressed together, the atoms on one surface can interact directly with atoms on the other surface, just like the clean copper blocks in the experiment. The surfaces begin to bond together at an atomic level — a phenomenon sometimes called cold welding.

Step 3 — Explain the result: Because of this direct atom-to-atom interaction, the friction coefficient rises far above the values seen in everyday conditions, making the components extremely hard to slide against each other. This matches exactly what was observed with the clean copper blocks, where the friction coefficient became much greater than one.

Step 4 — Suggest a solution: The engineer should apply a thin coating to the steel surfaces — for example, a dry lubricant such as molybdenum disulfide, which is commonly used in space applications. This coating acts as a chemical barrier between the two surfaces, preventing direct atomic contact and keeping friction at predictable, workable levels even in a vacuum where no natural oxide layer will form.

questions.q_text: A car of mass 1000 kilograms is travelling at 20 metres per second and needs to brake to a complete stop. On a dry road, the coefficient of friction between the tyre and road is 0.7. On a wet road, it drops to 0.4. Calculate the braking distance on each surface and explain the difference. Assume the braking force equals the friction force, and use the formula: braking distance equals speed squared divided by (2 times acceleration). Take gravitational acceleration as 10 metres per second squared.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Find the friction force on each surface. Friction force equals the coefficient of friction multiplied by the normal force. The normal force equals mass times gravitational acceleration, so 1000 times 10 equals 10,000 newtons. Dry friction force: 0.7 times 10,000 equals 7,000 newtons. Wet friction force: 0.4 times 10,000 equals 4,000 newtons. Step 2 — Find the deceleration on each surface using Newton's second law: acceleration equals force divided by mass. Dry deceleration: 7,000 divided by 1,000 equals 7 metres per second squared. Wet deceleration: 4,000 divided by 1,000 equals 4 metres per second squared. Step 3 — Calculate braking distance using: distance equals speed squared divided by (2 times deceleration). Dry: 20 squared divided by (2 times 7) equals 400 divided by 14, which is approximately 28.6 metres. Wet: 20 squared divided by (2 times 4) equals 400 divided by 8, which equals 50 metres. Step 4 — Interpret the result. The braking distance on a wet road (50 metres) is about 75 percent longer than on a dry road (28.6 metres). This is because the water film reduces direct rubber-to-concrete contact, lowering the coefficient of friction and therefore the maximum friction force available to slow the car.

questions.q_text: A book is sliding diagonally across a table — moving toward the upper-right corner. In which direction does kinetic friction act on the book?

questions.q_text: A 10 kilogram box sits on a flat floor. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor is 0.4, and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. You apply a horizontal force of 35 newtons to the box. Use g equals 10 meters per second squared. First, determine whether the box moves. If it does move, calculate the kinetic friction force acting on it.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Find the normal force. The floor is horizontal and the box is not accelerating vertically, so the normal force equals the weight of the box. Normal force = 10 kg times 10 m/s squared = 100 newtons.

Step 2 — Find the maximum static friction force. Maximum static friction = coefficient of static friction times normal force = 0.4 times 100 = 40 newtons.

Step 3 — Compare the applied force to the maximum static friction. The applied force is 35 newtons, which is less than 40 newtons. Therefore, static friction can match the applied force exactly, and the box does NOT move.

Step 4 — Since the box does not move, kinetic friction is not relevant here. The static friction force acting on the box is 35 newtons, directed opposite to the applied force.

Conclusion: The box remains stationary. Static friction = 35 newtons. Kinetic friction does not apply.

questions.q_text: A frying pan is coated with Teflon. Compared to an uncoated metal pan, why does food slide off the Teflon pan so much more easily?

questions.q_text: An engineer is designing a mechanical joint inside a medical device. The joint has two metal parts that must slide past each other thousands of times per day. The engineer is choosing between three surface options: leaving the metal surfaces bare, roughening them with sandpaper, or coating them with Teflon. Which option should the engineer choose, and why? Walk through the reasoning using what you know about friction and surface materials.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the goal. The joint must slide thousands of times per day, so the engineer wants to minimize friction. High friction would make sliding harder, waste energy, and wear the parts down quickly — especially important in a medical device where reliability matters.

Step 2 — Evaluate bare metal surfaces. Bare metal surfaces have a moderate coefficient of friction. They will resist sliding to a noticeable degree and will wear against each other over time, which is not ideal for a high-cycle application.

Step 3 — Evaluate roughened surfaces. Roughening the surfaces with sandpaper increases the microscopic peaks and valleys where the two surfaces interlock. This raises the coefficient of friction significantly, making sliding even harder and causing faster wear. This is the worst option for this goal.

Step 4 — Evaluate Teflon coating. Teflon has one of the lowest coefficients of friction of any known solid material. Coating the surfaces with Teflon means the two parts will slide past each other with very little resistance, reducing wear and energy loss. Teflon is also used in medical devices in real life precisely because it is safe, durable, and extremely slippery.

Conclusion — The engineer should choose the Teflon coating. It minimizes the friction force between the sliding parts, extends the life of the joint, and is appropriate for a medical context. This example illustrates that friction is a designable property: by selecting the right material, engineers can control how surfaces interact.

questions.q_text: A driver feels confident stopping quickly on dry concrete because of the high friction coefficient. She then drives onto a wet road and brakes with the same force. What should she expect, and why?

questions.q_text: A small delivery vehicle has a total weight of 12000 Newtons pressing down through its four tyres onto dry concrete. Using a coefficient of friction of 1.00 for rubber on dry concrete, calculate the maximum total friction force available to stop the vehicle. Then explain what would happen to this maximum friction force if the coefficient dropped to 0.40 on a wet road.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the formula. Friction force equals the coefficient of friction multiplied by the normal force pressing the surfaces together. In symbols: Friction force = coefficient times normal force.

Step 2 — Substitute the dry-road values. The normal force is 12000 Newtons and the coefficient is 1.00. So: Friction force = 1.00 times 12000 = 12000 Newtons.

Step 3 — Interpret the result. On dry concrete, the road can push back sideways with up to 12000 Newtons — equal to the full weight of the vehicle. This is what allows the brakes to stop the car effectively.

Step 4 — Apply the wet-road coefficient. If the coefficient drops to 0.40, the new maximum friction force = 0.40 times 12000 = 4800 Newtons.

Step 5 — Compare. On the wet road, the maximum friction force is only 4800 Newtons instead of 12000 Newtons — less than half. This means the brakes cannot slow the vehicle nearly as quickly, and the stopping distance increases substantially. This is why wet roads are so much more dangerous.

questions.q_text: A rubber tyre sits on dry concrete with a coefficient of friction of 1.00. If the tyre pushes down on the road with a force of 4000 Newtons, roughly what is the maximum sideways friction force the road can provide before the tyre starts to slip?

C. It means the friction force will always exactly equal the weight of the vehicle

questions.q_text: A steel ball falls through a jar of honey, and a wooden block slides across a concrete floor. In which of these two situations is the resistive force called a viscous force, and why?
options: A. The wooden block on concrete, because solid surfaces always produce viscous forces
B. The steel ball in honey, because at least one of the interacting substances is a fluid

questions.q_text: A heavy crate sits on a warehouse floor. You push on it with moderate force but it does not move. Which type of friction is acting on the crate, and why?

questions.q_text: A textbook rests on a ramp tilted at an angle. The ramp exerts a single contact force on the book. Explain how that one contact force gives rise to both a normal force and a friction force, and describe the direction of each component relative to the ramp surface.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the contact force. The ramp surface pushes on the book through electromagnetic interactions between their surfaces. This produces one overall contact force that can point at an angle to the ramp surface.

Step 2 — Decompose the contact force. Any force can be broken into perpendicular components. We choose directions that are useful: one direction perpendicular to the ramp surface, and one direction parallel to the ramp surface.

Step 3 — Name the components. The component of the contact force that points perpendicular to the ramp surface (directly away from the surface, into the book) is called the normal force. The component that points parallel to the ramp surface (along the slope, in this case directed up the slope to prevent the book from sliding down) is called friction.

Step 4 — Interpret physically. The normal force prevents the book from passing through the ramp. The friction force prevents the book from sliding down the incline. Together, these two components fully describe the single contact force the ramp exerts on the book. Since the book is not sliding, this friction is static friction.

questions.q_text: A student argues that if you polish two metal surfaces until they are perfectly smooth, friction between them should disappear entirely because there would be no bumps to create molecular bonds. What is the most important flaw in this reasoning?

B. Making surfaces extremely smooth actually increases the real contact area, allowing far more molecular bonds to form — which can make friction greater, not smaller

questions.q_text: A student rubs her hands together vigorously on a cold day and notices they feel warm. Using the atomic-level understanding of friction, explain step by step why rubbing produces warmth. Your answer should mention contact points, molecular bonds, and what happens to the energy involved.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Microscopic contact: Even though the palms look smooth, at the atomic scale both skin surfaces are covered in tiny bumps and valleys. When the hands are pressed together, only the tips of those bumps actually touch, forming a small number of real contact points.

Step 2 — Bond formation: At those contact points, atoms from each palm surface are extremely close together. Molecular attractive forces cause tiny bonds to form between the two surfaces right at those spots.

Step 3 — Bond breaking during sliding: When the student slides one hand across the other, she must apply a force large enough to break all those molecular bonds. Breaking bonds requires energy, which is supplied by the muscles doing the rubbing.

Step 4 — Deformation and vibrations: As each bond breaks, the material around the break point gets slightly disturbed and deformed. This disturbance spreads through the skin tissue as tiny mechanical vibration waves.

Step 5 — Conversion to heat: Those vibration waves gradually die out, and the energy they carried is transferred into the random, disordered motion of particles inside the skin. Increased random particle motion is precisely what we mean by a higher temperature — so the hands feel warm.

Step 6 — Continuous process: New bonds form immediately as the surfaces keep sliding, so the bond-breaking and energy conversion happen continuously as long as the rubbing continues, sustaining the warming effect.

questions.q_text: A furniture designer is building a wooden shelf unit that will sit on a wooden floor. She wants to know whether the shelf will tend to slide easily or resist sliding. Using the coefficient of friction for wood on wood, which is about 0.35, explain what this value tells her about the behaviour of her shelf, and compare it to what would happen if the coefficient were much lower, say 0.05.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Understand what the coefficient tells us. A coefficient of friction of 0.35 means there is a moderate level of resistance between the wooden shelf and the wooden floor. The shelf will not slide very easily — a reasonable amount of force is needed to move it. Step 2 — Interpret the value in context. Because 0.35 is a moderate number, the designer can expect the shelf to stay in place under normal conditions, such as when books are placed on it or when someone leans against it lightly. It will not slide across the room on its own. Step 3 — Compare to a coefficient of 0.05. A coefficient of 0.05 is very low, meaning the surfaces would be nearly frictionless — similar to something sliding on ice. If the shelf had this level of friction with the floor, it would slide very easily with almost any applied force, making it unsafe and unstable. Step 4 — Conclusion. The coefficient of 0.35 tells the designer that wood on wood provides a reasonable grip, making the shelf stable for everyday use. The higher the coefficient, the more the shelf resists sliding, which in this case is a desirable safety feature.
